vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: social-media-marketing-hub
Version: 7.1.0

The skill bundle contains hardcoded API credentials for TikHub and DeepSeek within `scripts/config.js`, which is a major security risk and poor practice. The main logic in `scripts/marketing_hub.js` performs high-risk system operations, including using `execSync` to construct and execute shell commands for launching `google-chrome` and `Xvfb` instances. While it attempts to sanitize inputs using `encodeURIComponent`, the pattern of building shell strings remains a significant vulnerability. Additionally, `scripts/cmd_vid_integration.py` attempts to execute scripts from a different skill's directory (`chanjing-one-click-video-creation`), creating an undocumented and potentially unsafe cross-skill dependency.

llm.summary: The skill mostly does what it says (social-media analysis + AI generation) but contains clear inconsistencies and risky items — including hard-coded API keys, subprocess commands (Xvfb/Chrome/pkill) not reflected in declared permissions, and code that can invoke other local skill scripts — so proceed with caution.

dimensions.detail: High-level purpose (TikTok/XHS/Ks analysis + AI generation) matches the code and documentation. However, the packaged repo already contains actual API keys in scripts/config.js (TIKHUB_TOKEN and DEEPSEEK_KEY) despite the manifest declaring no required env vars and marking config.js as doNotCommitToVcs. Embedding live credentials in the shipped files is inconsistent and dangerous.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs cloning and running the Node script (consistent), but the runtime code does more than described: it will make HTTPS calls to third-party APIs, try to launch or spawn system-level processes (Xvfb, google-chrome), run pkill, and may call other local skill scripts (cmd_vid_integration.py references a path under ~/.openclaw-agent2/... and will attempt to execute run_render.py if present). Those actions expand scope beyond simple 'API calls + local file writes' and are not clearly documented in the top-level instructions.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: No formal install spec in manifest (skill is packaged with source). SKILL.md suggests git-clone from GitHub, which is a normal distribution method. There are no downloads from unknown URLs or archive extraction. Overall install mechanism is low-risk, but the package itself contains code that executes system-level commands at runtime.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Manifest declares no required environment variables, but scripts/config.js contains hard-coded tokens (including a string starting with 'sk-'), meaning the skill ships with credentials baked in. The manifest allows network access to api.tikhub.io and api.deepseek.com, which matches purpose, but code executes arbitrary shell commands (execSync) to manage Xvfb and Chrome — these are not reflected in subprocess allowedPatterns (manifest lists only node). The python integration script references a path in the user's home directory (other skill), which is outside declared read roots. These mismatches indicate insufficient or misleading declaration of required secrets and system access.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: Skill is not marked always:true and does not claim to modify other skills. However, it attempts to interact with other local components if present (chanjing run_render.py) and will write workflows and memory files under the skill workspace. The manifest's claimed subprocess pattern and filesystem allowances do not fully reflect the actual runtime behavior (spawning Xvfb/Chrome/pkill and referencing home-directory skill paths), increasing privilege/impact risk if run in an agent with broader access.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to consider before installing or running this skill:

1) Hard-coded credentials: scripts/config.js contains what appear to be real API keys (TIKHUB_TOKEN and DEEPSEEK_KEY). That is a red flag — either the keys were accidentally committed (bad hygiene) or the package author is shipping working credentials (also bad). Do NOT trust or use those keys. Replace them with your own tokens and rotate any leaked keys.

2) Subprocess and system commands: the Node code uses child_process.execSync to run system commands (pkill, Xvfb, and google-chrome) and will try to launch a browser. The manifest's allowed subprocess patterns only list node, so the declared permissions are incomplete. If you run this skill, do so in a sandboxed environment (container/VM) where starting X servers or killing processes is safe.

3) Cross-skill/local-script invocation: the Python helper looks for and will invoke a run_render.py script in ~/.openclaw-agent2/... — that means the skill may call other local code if present. If you have other skills installed, be aware this may trigger them. Confirm you trust or isolate that other code.

4) Network endpoints: the skill communicates with api.tikhub.io and api.deepseek.com (documented). Confirm you are comfortable sending search queries and any scraped data to those services. If DeepSeek uses an OpenAI-style key (sk-...), treat it as sensitive.

5) Inconsistencies to resolve before trusting: ask the author (or verify yourself) that the included config.js keys are test/dummy keys; update the manifest to list the real subprocess commands the code will run; remove embedded credentials; and confirm the intent/behavior of the chrome/Xvfb logic. If the repo author cannot or will not fix these, prefer running the code only in an isolated environment after manual code review.

6) Quick mitigation steps: inspect and delete scripts/config.js before running; configure your own API keys via the documented config command; run the skill in a sandbox/container that restricts network and system-level commands; and search the code for any other hard-coded secrets or unexpected remote endpoints.

If you want, I can highlight the exact lines/files to edit (e.g., remove/rotate config.js keys, disable auto Xvfb startup) or produce a safe-run checklist and a minimal wrapper script to restrict subprocess calls.
